clinicalPearls: AApoAI is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the APOA1 gene, whose product is the principal apolipoprotein of high-density lipoprotein.
It is a multi-organ hereditary amyloidosis in which the pattern of organ involvement is strongly determined by the specific mutation and its position within the protein.
Common targets include the kidney, liver, heart, larynx, skin and testes, with hepatic and renal involvement frequently dominant.
N-terminal mutations tend to cause hepatic and renal disease, whereas C-terminal mutations more often affect the heart, larynx and skin, providing a useful genotype-phenotype guide.
Progression is typically slow, and life expectancy may be near-normal in many kindreds despite organ deposition.
Hepatic involvement can cause marked cholestasis and hepatomegaly, while renal involvement is often tubulointerstitial rather than purely glomerular, with modest proteinuria.
Organ transplantation of kidney or liver is used for advanced single-organ failure, and outcomes are generally favourable given the indolent course.
reference.pathophysiology: Amyloidogenic variants of apolipoprotein A-I, generated by mutations in APOA1, are cleaved to release an N-terminal fragment that misfolds and aggregates into amyloid fibrils. Because apolipoprotein A-I is central to high-density lipoprotein metabolism and is expressed in the liver and intestine, variant protein circulates widely and deposits in multiple tissues, with the precise tropism dictated by the mutation. Renal deposition is often concentrated in the medulla and interstitium, producing slowly progressive renal impairment with relatively modest proteinuria, while hepatic deposits cause cholestasis. The generally slow kinetics of deposition account for the comparatively indolent clinical course.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary amyloidoses (fibrinogen, lysozyme, LECT2, transthyretin)
Other causes of chronic kidney disease
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy of the affected organ with Congo red staining
Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry and immunohistochemistry
Renal and liver function with quantified proteinuria
Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis
SAP scintigraphy to assess organ burden
Echocardiography and laryngoscopy where the mutation predicts cardiac or laryngeal disease
redFlags: Unexplained cholestatic liver disease with hepatomegaly
Progressive renal impairment with a supportive family history
Hoarseness or airway symptoms suggesting laryngeal amyloid
Family history of multi-organ disease or premature organ failure
reference.prognosis: The course is usually indolent with slow organ deterioration and often near-normal survival. Targeted organ transplantation can provide durable benefit for isolated advanced renal or hepatic failure.
pitfalls: Mistyping as AL amyloidosis and giving unnecessary chemotherapy
Attributing cholestasis to primary liver disease
Underestimating renal involvement because proteinuria is modest
Failing to offer genetic counselling and family screening
